month.note: This figure describes gross (before-tax) income, not take-home pay. It was filed on the net topic and has been demoted rather than published, because break-even must compare money out against money that actually reaches the worker. Using gross here would roughly halve the reported months in most European countries.

net_monthly_income.note: career.net_monthly_income: a net-income figure must declare the circumstances it holds under. Missing: dependents (Number of dependents claimed, or an explicit statement that none are claimed. A household-level median silently averages different household tax positions together.); employee_social_contributions (Whether pension, health and unemployment contributions are deducted from this figure, and which. Some systems have no such deduction; Singapore's CPF is a large deduction that never reaches the worker.); marital_status (Single or married. Usually the largest single adjustment to take-home pay, and a family fact rather than an employment fact.); per (needed for a period to exist); residency (Resident or non-resident status, where the jurisdiction distinguishes them. Several systems tax residents and non-residents differently.). Defaulting any of these would publish a confident number for a household, tax year or residency status nobody stated.

sources.notes:
Bachelor tuition for Finland, from a named university's own fee page. The University of Helsinki states a single figure: 'The fee for the English-language bachelor's programmes is 13,000 EUR per academic year.' That is PER ACADEMIC YEAR, not per semester, and it is a flat single figure for the English-language Bachelor's programmes rather than a banded range. The Master's range (13,000/15,000/18,000) is recorded here only to demonstrate that the Bachelor figure is not part of a band; the brief's rule against inferring Master's funding means the Master's fees are context, not a claim for this metric.

WHO PAYS. The university states liability as 'non-EU/non-EEA students studying in English in Master's or Bachelor's degree programme', with exemptions for EU/EEA/Swiss citizens and holders of certain Finnish residence statuses including a permanent residence card. Note the university flags that a continuous residence permit (type A) does NOT exempt a student where it was granted on the basis of studying.

MATERIAL FINDING FOR A SCHOLARSHIP CORPUS, and it belongs here rather than in a file about the myth, because it changes what a Bachelor applicant in Finland faces: 'There are no tuition fee waivers for applicants applying for the English-language Bachelor's degrees.' So a non-EU Bachelor applicant at Helsinki pays the full 13,000 EUR per year with no fee-waiver route through the university's own scheme. The only mention is a Dean's award of 1.000 EUR (European decimal notation: EUR 1,000) for second and third year students based on prior academic performance, which is a performance award, not a means-based waiver. This corroborates the Finnish National Agency for Education's statement that such aid is institutional and tuition-only, and here it is tuition-only AND not available at Bachelor entry.

CORROBORATION AND A DISCREPANCY ON THE BAND, from a second official source fetched in this session (https://www.studyinfinland.fi/funding-your-studies/fees-and-cost-living, the Finnish National Agency for Education): 'Tuition fees typically range from EUR 9,000 to EUR 20,000 per year, depending on the university and programme.' Helsinki's 13,000 sits inside that national range. No conflict, but note the national page's lower bound differs from what a student might expect: Finland's per-student Bachelor tuition is materially higher than the historical EUR 800 minimum that circulated in older material, and the agency page also states 'Degree programmes taught in Finnish or Swedish do not charge tuition fees', which is the genuine zero-fee route for a Finnish-taught Bachelor.

The '13,000' is University of Helsinki specifically. Novia and the University of Turku, per pages I saw only in search index rather than as fetched pages, are not recorded here because I did not fetch them.

sources.notes:
Financial proof for Finland, EUR 800 per month. IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden: this page is the Finnish National Agency for Education's Study in Finland site, and the agency is RELAYING the number rather than setting it. Its words are 'the official minimum requirement set by Finnish Immigration Service Migri is EUR 800 per month (EUR 9,600 per year)'. The requirement is therefore MIGRI's, and the authoritative source is the Finnish Immigration Service. I attempted https://migri.fi/en/income-requirement-for-students, which the page links to as the place to prove sufficient finances, and the fetch FAILED with a timeout. I also received HTTP 403 on migri.fi earlier in this session. So the figure below is attested by one official government publisher quoting another official authority, at second hand. It is solid but it is not the primary document, and that distinction should survive into whatever canonical file consumes it.

The page gives both the monthly figure and the annual derivation (EUR 9,600 per year), which is convenient because the annual form is what a first-year cost model needs and here it does not require my own arithmetic.

ESTIMATE, CLEARLY LABELLED: the EUR 900-EUR 1,200 per month recommended figure is explicitly the agency's recommendation for actual living expenses, not a legal threshold. Anything derived from that range must carry an ESTIMATE marker.

ALSO RECORDED, all verbatim from this page, because a first-year budget needs them and they are small enough to be lost by rounding: student union membership about EUR 50-EUR 70 per academic year; FSHS student healthcare fee currently around EUR 35 per term, about EUR 70 per year, payable to Kela and required for Bachelor's and Master's students.

WORK RIGHTS, from this same official page: international students 'are allowed to work part-time up to 30 hours per week on average during the academic year and full-time during holidays.' This is a markedly more permissive figure than Sweden's new 15-hour cap, and the two should not be conflated. The agency adds the practical caution that such wages 'would not be sufficient to cover both tuition and living costs', i.e. part-time work is not a funding plan.

sources.notes:
Finland's post-study job-search permit, duration TWO YEARS, and the page states it in general terms without restricting it to Master's graduates: 'Finland offers a two-year post-study permit which allows you to look for work or start a business.' Since it is written as available to anyone who graduates and stays to search for employment, it is stated at Bachelor's level here. That is the plain reading and it is generous: two years is among the longest job-search windows in this corpus.

SECONDARY-SOURCE CAVEAT, because it matters. This is the Finnish National Agency for Education's Study in Finland site, not Migri. The page itself points to the primary source: 'Find more information about the post-study permit on Migri.fi', linking https://migri.fi/en/after-graduation. I did NOT successfully fetch Migri. migri.fi returned HTTP 403 on an earlier attempt in this session and a request timeout on another. So the two-year figure is attested by an official national publisher that names the primary authority, but the primary page itself was not read by me. It should be confirmed against Migri before being treated as settled in a canonical file. I am recording the gap rather than concealing it.

Also worth noting for a scholarship corpus: the same page's emphasis on language and on university career services implies the permit is worth less without Finnish or Swedish. That is the agency's guidance rather than a rule, and I record it as a note, not a claim.

sources.notes:
THE FINNISH SCHOLARSHIP MYTH IS CONFIRMED, from the national agency itself, and the confirmation is stronger than the brief anticipated. The Finnish National Agency for Education states flatly: 'Scholarships and tuition fee waivers in Finland are offered by individual universities. There are no governmental scholarship programmes available.'

That is a broader statement than 'no Bachelor's-level government scholarship'. It says there is NO Finnish governmental scholarship programme for any level. The agency also names the specific myth in its own fact-check panel: 'You may have seen posts and ads promoting "Fully funded Finland government scholarships" that would cover everything from university tuition fees to travel and living costs in Finland. Be cautious - those claims are misleading. Posts and ads like that contain a lot of false information.'

So the widely-repeated 'Finnish Government Scholarship' for Bachelor's study is not merely unsupported at Bachelor level; the national agency actively labels such advertising false.

CORROBORATED ON A SECOND OFFICIAL PAGE, fetched in this session: https://www.oph.fi/en/education-development/support-programmes-foreigners-studying-finland, titled 'Scholarship programmes for Doctoral-level studies and research in Finland'. That page carries no Bachelor's or Master's scholarship programme at all and records that 'EDUFI Fellowship for foreign doctoral researchers will end at the end of 2025. New applications cannot be submitted after 17.10.2025.' and 'EDUFI Fellowship for doctoral students from Ukraine has ended and applications for it are no longer being accepted.' The agency is, as of 2026, winding down even its doctoral schemes.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXISTS, therefore, is INSTITUTIONAL aid only: university-offered scholarships and tuition-fee waivers, which the agency says 'typically only cover your tuition fees, either partially or wholly' and never living costs. That is the honest Bachelor funding picture for Finland: a Bachelor-level international student should be modelled as self-funding tuition plus self-funding living costs.

CAUTION AGAINST A SYMMETRICAL ERROR: the absence of a Finnish government scholarship must not be read as 'Finland has no scholarship'. The University of Helsinki page I fetched does describe a Master's scholarship programme (50% and 100% tuition-fee waivers) and notes a limited pathway where a Bachelor's graduate continuing to a Master's can be awarded a waiver. None of that is Bachelor's-level.

RESOLVED AFTER FETCHING THE LINKED FACT-CHECK PAGE. I did fetch /news-events/scholarship-facts separately, and it is quoted in full as Source B above. It is the strongest form of the debunking: 'The truth is, there are no governmental scholarships for bachelor's or master's studies in Finland.' It also gives the mechanism of the scam, noting such ads 'may also use Finnish authorities' logos without permission', which matters because a corpus collecting Finnish scholarship claims will keep encountering logo-bearing advertorials that look governmental.

The two sources agree. There is no conflict.
